title: Characterizing COVID-19 Content Posted to TikTok: Public Sentiment and Response During the First Phase of the COVID-19 Pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of 750 randomly selected TikTok videos tagged #coronavirus (Jan-Mar 2020), human-coded against CDC guidance: 27% of videos were identified as having incorrect, misleading or incomplete information about COVID-19. A quantitative share of items with a clear denominator, judged against an external ground truth (CDC guidelines), so CONTENT rather than QUALITY.

estimates.country: Not stated (TikTok videos worldwide; non-English videos were not translated; authors are US-based)
estimates.date: Videos posted January, February and March 2020; extracted on February 4, March 6 and April 2, 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of #coronavirus TikTok videos coded as containing incorrect, misleading or incomplete information about COVID-19
estimates.value_raw: Twenty-seven percent of videos were identified as having incorrect, misleading, or incomplete information about COVID-19; by month n = 77 (32%) January, n = 64 (27%) February, n = 37 (20%) March of 250 videos each
estimates.denominator: 750 TikTok videos tagged #coronavirus (250 randomly selected from each of January, February and March 2020, drawn from a pool of 2,676 extracted videos)
estimates.definition: Video coded under “Narrative reliability” as “Incorrect/Misleading”, operationally defined as “Not in accordance with fact or omitted facts”; examples of misleading information given were how to properly wear personal protective equipment, how COVID-19 is spread, or incorrect statistics about spread and mortality, with coders consulting CDC guidelines
estimates.misinfo_def: “Misleading information included how to properly wear personal protective equipment, how COVID-19 is spread, or incorrect statistics about spread and mortality. Coders consulted the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines to determine and confirm ‘misleading information.’”
estimates.source_quote: Narrative reliability Twenty-seven percent of videos were identified as having incorrect, misleading, or incomplete information about COVID-19 ( Table 1 Figure 1 .). Videos posted in January had the highest proportion of misleading information (n = 77, 32%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, “Narrative reliability”; Table 1 (Incorrect/Misleading row); restated in Discussion (“more than a quarter (27%) of videos”)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Three reviewers (ES, LS, BB) coded each video in REDCap using an iteratively developed codebook (built on 2 x 50 January videos); “The final code for each video was decided by the agreement between three reviewers”; coders consulted CDC guidelines to determine and confirm misleading information. No kappa or other inter-rater reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used #Coronavirus to extract TikTok videos on February 4, March 6, and April 2, 2020, for a total sample of 2,676 videos. ... Our sample included 250 randomly selected TikTok videos from each month, January, February, and March 2020, representing a total sample of 750 videos.
estimates.notes: Time series collapsed to the paper's own headline overall figure (27% across the full Jan-Mar 2020 period) rather than the three monthly points. ADJUDICATOR NOTE — internal arithmetic inconsistency in the paper: the monthly misleading counts (77 + 64 + 37 = 178) give 23.7% of 750, not 27%; Table 2's monthly percentages for the same counts (36.10%, 27.47%, 20.22%) also disagree with Table 1's (32%, 27%, 20% of 250). The 27% is stated verbatim twice (Results and Discussion) and is the figure the abstract/discussion carries, so it is kept per R8, but the true value may be ~24%. The category bundles “incomplete” with “incorrect/misleading”, so breadth=misleading (broadest). Country is not stated: hashtag-based global TikTok sample, non-English videos not translated.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 17% (n = 115) coded “intended to inform” — accurate/informative content, not misinformation; (b) the Table 2 breakdown of themes WITHIN misleading/incorrect videos (humor, fear, expose, racial comment, etc.) — these are sentiment/production attributes of the misinformation subsample, not falsity shares, so no R3 within-misinfo row applies; (c) mean shares and comments for misleading vs all videos (Table 3) — engagement counts, not a share of shares that are misinformation and not a per-capita exposure intensity of misinformation; (d) “less than 1% provided misleading or inaccurate health advice” and “nearly one-third of respondents younger than the age of 25 years (28%) believe that humans originally contracted COVID-19 by eating bats” — both figures the paper cites from other studies (Ostrovsky & Chen 2020; Baum et al. 2020), excluded by R8; (e) monthly sub-points of the same time series (32% / 27% / 20%), collapsed into the representative overall value.

rob.design: Retrospective observational content analysis. Sampling frame: publicly available TikTok videos tagged #coronavirus, extracted on three dates (4 Feb, 6 Mar, 2 Apr 2020) for a pool of 2,676 videos, from which 250 videos per month were randomly selected (N = 750). Coding: iteratively developed REDCap codebook (narrative reliability, misleading information, production, sentiment, content), all sub-theme codes mutually exclusive, final code by agreement of three reviewers, CDC guidelines used as the accuracy standard. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported; no response-rate concept (content study). Limitations acknowledged by the authors: single hashtag only, no control over TikTok's ranking algorithm, non-English videos not translated, videos coded without their captions, short window (Jan-Mar 2020).
